title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
description:
A **trie** (prefix tree) stores a set of strings so that any prefix can be looked up in time proportional to its length, independent of how many words are stored.

Implement the class:

- `Trie()` creates an empty trie.
- `insert(word)` adds `word` to the trie.
- `search(word)` returns `true` if exactly `word` was inserted earlier.
- `startsWith(prefix)` returns `true` if at least one inserted word begins with `prefix`.

All strings consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: After inserting "apple", "app" is a prefix but not a stored word, so search("app") is false while startsWith("app") is true. Inserting "app" makes search("app") true.

constraints: Strings contain only lowercase letters a-z.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls in total to insert, search and startsWith.
hints: Each node represents one prefix; its children are the possible next letters.
Walk one character at a time from the root. insert creates missing children; search and startsWith stop and return false at the first missing child.
The only difference between search and startsWith is that search also requires an 'end of word' flag on the final node.
approach:
**One node per prefix, one edge per letter.** The root represents the empty string. Each node has a map from next character to child node and a flag marking whether the path from the root to it spells a complete inserted word. Every operation is a walk of at most `len(s)` steps.

- `insert`: walk, creating children as needed; mark the final node as a word.
- `startsWith`: walk; succeed if the walk never hits a missing child.
- `search`: same walk, but additionally require the end-of-word flag.

**Why the flag matters:** "app" is a prefix of "apple", so the node for "app" exists after inserting "apple". Without the flag, `search("app")` would wrongly return true.

**Children as dict vs fixed array:** a dict is simplest and memory-proportional to what is used; an array of 26 slots is faster and what many interviewers expect you to mention for a fixed alphabet.

**Common mistakes:** marking every node on the path as a word; sharing a single root-level dict so that search and startsWith become identical; using a set of all prefixes instead (correct but O(total length) memory and missing the point of the question).

**Interview follow-ups:** delete a word (walk down, then prune childless non-word nodes on the way back up); count words with a given prefix (store a counter on each node); autocomplete the k most frequent completions (DFS from the prefix node, or cache top-k per node); memory optimisation with a compressed (radix) trie.

complexity.time: O(L) per operation, L = length of the string
